title: Referring words
subtitle: problem, issue, approach, solution
summary: Use text-referring words such as problem, issue, question, approach and solution to organise an argument and point back to what has just been said.

lesson.heading: What are text-referring words?
lesson.text: Some words take their meaning from the text around them. On its own, 'We decided to look at the **problem** again and try to find a **solution**' tells you nothing about the topic. **Problem** and **solution** organise the argument; they refer to something said somewhere else.

examples.text: Pollution is increasing. The **problem** is getting worse each day.
Should taxes be raised or lowered? This was the biggest **issue** in the election.
examples.note: issue = a topic causing great argument and controversy

examples.text: Whether the war could have been avoided is a **question** that interests historians.
Let's discuss crime. That's always an interesting **topic**.
examples.note: topic = a subject to argue about or discuss, e.g. in a debate or an essay

examples.text: Punishment is only one **aspect** of crime.
examples.note: aspect = one part of the topic

lesson.heading: Problem-solution word families
lesson.note: Learn these as a family: a text often moves from situation to problem to response to solution to evaluation.

lesson.heading: A problem-solution text
lesson.text: In this kind of writing a problem is presented and ways of solving it are discussed. Notice how each word in bold refers back to what came before it.

examples.text: The **situation** in our cities with regard to traffic is going from bad to worse.
Congestion is a daily feature of urban life. The **problem** is now beginning to affect our national economies.
Unless a new **approach** is found to control traffic, we will never find a **solution** to the **dilemma**.

lesson.heading: Words that refer to parts of an argument
lesson.text: In a debate, words like **claim**, **fact**, **argument**, **position**, **point** and **view** label what the other speaker has just said - and often judge it at the same time.

examples.text: *A:* Your **claim** that we're doing nothing to invest in industry is false. We invested ten billion last year. You've ignored this **fact**.
*B:* But the investment has all gone to service industries. The real **point** is that we need to invest in our manufacturing industries.
*A:* That **argument** is out-of-date. Our **position** has always been that we should encourage technology.
*B:* But that **view** won't help to reduce unemployment.

lesson.heading: From situation to evaluation
lesson.text: Here is the whole chain in one short text. Each word in bold picks up the stage before it.

examples.text: Economically, the government is in a critical **position**. This **state of affairs** is partly a result of the financial **difficulties** currently being experienced globally.
Our government's initial **response** to the situation was to impose higher taxes.
This **approach** has not proved to be the **solution** to the problem. Economists' current **assessment** is that this may in fact be making **matters** worse.

lesson.heading: Choosing the right label
rows: something someone holds to be true without proof
a topic people argue and disagree about
a judgment of how well something works
a difficult choice between two options

lesson.text: When you start an essay paragraph with *This problem*, *That approach* or *Such a situation*, check that the reader can see exactly which words you are referring back to.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the label that best describes it.

pairs.left: The earth is in orbit around the sun.
It has proved to be most efficient.
They should get married, to my mind.

exercises.prompt: So you were talking about animal rights? That's quite a big ___ nowadays.
exercises.explanation: An issue is a topic that causes argument and controversy.

exercises.prompt: We are running out of funds. How do you propose we should deal with the ___?
exercises.explanation: Problem or matter both refer back to the difficulty just described; crisis if it is really serious.

exercises.prompt: Is there life on other planets? This is a ___ nobody has yet been able to answer.
exercises.explanation: A question is something that can be asked and answered; mystery is also possible here.

exercises.prompt: You can write your essay on 'My best holiday ever'. If you don't like that ___, I'll give you another one.
exercises.hint: (a subject to write or talk about)
exercises.explanation: A topic is a subject for an essay or a discussion.

exercises.prompt: She thinks we should all fly around in tiny little helicopters. This ___ to the traffic problem in cities is rather new and unusual.
exercises.explanation: Approach and response take to, as does solution and answer.

exercises.prompt: Match each newspaper headline with the text extract that belongs to it.

pairs.right: ... she said if the world community failed to respond, thousands of children could die
... tests were being carried out to see if the new drug really did work

pairs.left: SCIENTIST REJECTS CLAIMS OVER FAST FOOD
pairs.right: ... there was no proof at all that such things were harmful

pairs.left: SOLUTION TO AGE-OLD MYSTERY IN KENYA
pairs.right: ... the bones proved beyond doubt that human beings had inhabited the region

pairs.left: PRIME MINISTER SETS OUT VIEWS ON NATO

exercises.prompt: Sort these words into the family they belong to.
Which word means 'part of a topic'?
exercises.explanation: Punishment is only one aspect of crime - one part of the whole topic.

exercises.prompt: Which is the more formal word for a problem?
exercises.explanation: Difficulty belongs to the same family as problem but is more formal.

exercises.prompt: Which preposition normally follows *state of affairs* and *position* when you say what they concern?
exercises.explanation: The situation / position with regard to traffic is going from bad to worse.

exercises.statement: Economists' current assessment is that higher taxes may be making matters worse.
exercises.explanation: Correct - an assessment is an evaluation of how well a solution is working.

exercises.statement: A *dilemma* is a fact that everyone accepts as true.
exercises.explanation: A dilemma is a difficult choice between two options; a fact is something known to be true.
